resources.string: Heart rate during the night, average %1$d, lowest %2$d bpm

How restorative the night was: what decides how rested and able you are today. Two parts, both measured on this night alone.

# Graded, not pass or fail
Every measure is graded around its published threshold. Just meeting the threshold earns 60 % of its points; better values earn more, up to full points at an excellent value.

# The parts
- Duration, 60 points: time asleep against your need, your usual sleep kept between 7 and 9 hours. Full points at your need, 60 % at 85 % of it, none at 60 %. Sleep restriction impairs the next day's attention and performance in proportion to the shortfall (Van Dongen 2003; Belenky 2003).
- Continuity, 40 points: the National Sleep Foundation's quality criteria as thresholds. Awake after falling asleep 20 minutes (excellent 5) for two thirds of the points, one long awakening of 5 minutes or more (excellent none) for a third. Broken sleep impairs the next day much like short sleep (Stepanski 2002).

# Time awake in bed
The night runs from falling asleep to the final awakening. Time awake in bed before and after does not count: the watch cannot tell reading in bed from trying to sleep, and lying in after waking says nothing about the sleep. For the same reason the Foundation's other two criteria, time to fall asleep and the share of time in bed spent asleep, are left out: both count from the moment you try to sleep.

# Habits are scored apart
Regularity, the time of night and your usual amount of sleep matter for long-term health, but they are habits rather than properties of one night. Sleep health scores them over two weeks.

# What is not scored
- Sleep stages: wrist sensors tell them apart only roughly, and one night's shares say little about its quality.
- Brief arousals: they are a normal part of healthy sleep.

# Ratings
- 80 and above: good
- 65 to 79: fair
- Below 65: poor

# Compared with Fitbit
Fitbit's score also counts deep and REM sleep, restlessness and sleeping heart rate, with weights it does not publish, so the two can differ by 10 points or more. Resting heart rate and HRV count in readiness instead.

Your sleep habits over the last two weeks, the dimensions of sleep health a watch can measure (Buysse 2014). Composite scores of these dimensions predict health and mortality (Wallace 2018; Brindle 2019); here each counts a quarter. It needs 5 nights in the two weeks.

# The parts
- Regularity: the Sleep Regularity Index (Phillips 2017), the chance of being asleep or awake at the same moment on consecutive days, from 100 (the same times every day) down. Excellent from 87, threshold 74, nothing below 50. In 61,000 UK Biobank participants the median was 81, and regularity predicted mortality more strongly than duration (Windred 2024). Only the main sleep counts; naps are not recorded.
- Duration: your average time asleep against your need. Threshold 90 %, full points at your need, nothing below 75 %. Habitually short sleep raises the risk of disease (Cappuccio 2010).
- Continuity: the ease of falling asleep and of getting back to sleep. The watch cannot see when you start trying to sleep, so this is the time awake after falling asleep on a typical night (the median). Threshold 20 minutes, excellent 5, nothing from 50.
- Timing: the usual middle of the night within 02:00 to 04:00. 60 % an hour outside it, nothing beyond two and a half hours.

# Sleep debt (the tile)
Sleep missed against your need over the last two weeks, as Oura and WHOOP show it. Each night's shortfall counts, last night fully and two weeks ago a fourteenth, because recent sleep loss weighs on today more. A night longer than your need pays back half its surplus: recovery sleep restores performance only partly (Belenky 2003; Banks 2010). Nights without a record are skipped. Levels follow Oura: low under 2 hours, moderate 2 to 5, high over 5.

The stages as your watch estimated them from movement and heart rate, one lane per stage, from falling asleep to the final awakening. Time awake in bed before and after is left out.

- Deep sleep: the most restorative stage, mostly early in the night.
- REM sleep: dreaming sleep, longer towards the morning.
- Light sleep: about half of a normal night.
- Awake: short awakenings are normal; several a night are part of healthy sleep.
- Restless: brief awakenings of a minute or a few, too short for the awake stage. Fitbit shares them only through the Google Health API, so the lane shows once it is connected. They are shown, not scored: brief arousals are part of normal sleep, and a wrist sensor finds them only roughly.

The line under the headline names what held the night back most: the measures below their threshold, or, on a good night, the ones furthest from excellent.

How the night compares with published ranges. The tinted band on each bar is the range, the dot the night.

- Awake after falling asleep and long awakenings: the National Sleep Foundation's sleep quality recommendations (Ohayon 2017). Its other two, time to fall asleep and sleep efficiency, count from the moment you try to sleep, which the watch cannot tell from reading in bed, so they are left out.
- Deep and REM sleep: typical shares for healthy adults. Compared with a sleep lab, wrist sensors misplace a good part of stage time, so these two are shown but not scored.

Heart rate from falling asleep to the final awakening, averaged over five minutes and smoothed over a quarter of an hour, so that turning over or a brief awakening does not dominate the line.

- Average: the mean over the whole night.
- Lowest: the calmest quarter of an hour.
- Resting: the resting heart rate your watch derived from the night, drawn as a line.

Heart rate usually falls through the first half of the night. A night that stays well above your usual, or does not fall, often follows hard training late in the day, alcohol, a big late meal or the start of an illness.

Measured while you slept and compared with your own nights: the range is where 80 % of your nights fell, from the 60 nights before for HRV and the 30 before for the others, once there are 14 nights. Tap a row for its history.

- HRV: the median of the watch's five-minute values, as Fitbit reports it, or Fitbit's own nightly value when the Google Health API is connected. Without it, when the values cover less than 60 % of the time asleep (Fitbit sometimes shares only the first hours of a night), the night has no HRV rather than a wrong one.
- Resting heart rate: as your watch derived it from the night.
- Breathing rate: breaths per minute during sleep. A rise of a breath or more above usual is a common early sign of illness.
- SpO2 and skin temperature: only with the Google Health API connected. SpO2 is the night's average oxygen saturation; skin temperature is the difference from Fitbit's own baseline for you.

# Several at once
Any measure leaves its range now and then. When two or more do on the same night, the line at the top warns, as Apple's Vitals app does: an illness starting, alcohol, travel or a hard block of training are the usual reasons. It is a prompt to take it easy, not a diagnosis.

The last 7 or 30 nights up to the night shown, with the average beside each chart. Tinted bands are healthy targets from sleep research: a good score, your sleep need, at most 20 minutes awake after falling asleep and the typical deep and REM shares for adults. They stay fixed on purpose: a habit of short or shallow sleep should not come to look normal. Values outside the band turn orange.

HRV, resting heart rate and breathing rate are different: healthy values vary so much between people that they are compared with your own usual instead.

Sleep times show one bar per night from falling asleep to the final awakening; bars that line up mean a regular rhythm.
You felt %2$s in the morning (%1$d of 5)
How rested do you feel this morning?
How rested did you feel on %1$s?

The question at the top is for the morning after the night shown: Today asks it until you answer, and here you can change an answer or give one you missed. Tap your answer again to clear it.

Each dot is a morning: the sleep score of the night across, how rested you said you felt up the side. The ringed dot is the morning shown. The tick in a row marks its median score.

# Agreement
Spearman's rank correlation between score and answer, from −1 to 1. Near 1 the score rises with how rested you feel, near 0 it does not follow your feeling, below 0 it runs against it. It uses only the order of your answers, not equal steps between them. The words follow Evans (1996): from 0.2 weak, from 0.4 moderate, from 0.6 strong.

It shows from 10 mornings. With few mornings it is uncertain: at ten it takes about 0.65 to rule out chance, at thirty about 0.36.

A weak agreement means the score misses something you feel, such as stress, illness or a late meal, or weighs something you do not notice. The score's parts and weights come from published sleep health criteria, not from your answers.

When you sleep before workdays and before free days, from the last four weeks of nights. It follows the Munich ChronoType Questionnaire (Roenneberg 2003), with the nights your watch recorded instead of answers.

- Chronotype: the middle of your sleep before free days, when no alarm sets the end, corrected for catching up. If you sleep longer then, half of the extra beyond your weekly average is taken off (Roenneberg 2004). Surveys put the average adult between about 3:00 and 4:00 (Czech and Japanese samples: 3:08 and 3:42), later in young adults. Here before 3:00 counts as early and from 5:00 as late.
- Social jetlag: how far the middle of your sleep moves between workdays and free days (Wittmann 2006). About two thirds of people have an hour or more and a third two hours or more; more of it goes with higher odds of being overweight (Roenneberg 2012). Under an hour is low, from two hours high.

A night counts as free when the day after it is one of your free days: Saturday and Sunday unless you change them in Settings, Sleep. The bars show the average night of each kind, from falling asleep to waking, with its middle marked.
The morning question, and your answers against the score
What goes with better and worse nights, measured and felt

What goes with your better and worse nights, from your own data: the sleep score, and how rested you said you felt in the morning (switch at the top). There is nothing to log: the factors come from your training, your sleep times and what the watch measures.

# Reading the chart
- Each row is a factor. The dot is its likely effect for the typical change named in the row, with every other factor held equal: to the right better, to the left worse.
- The bar spans the middle 80 % of what the effect could be. The grey band around zero marks effects too small to matter: under a point of score, or a tenth of a step of the rating.
- A coloured row is clear: its whole bar lies beyond the grey band, so it is at least 90 % likely to be worth more than that. Grey rows are not clear yet.
- Tap a row to see your nights split by that factor.

# The factors
- Before the night: training load in the 24 hours before falling asleep, training that ended less than 4 hours before (Stutz 2019; Leota 2025), form going into the day, when you fell asleep, the night before against your need, and whether the next morning is a free day.
- During the night, for feeling rested only: time asleep against your need, time awake after falling asleep, and deep sleep in the last half hour before waking, when grogginess is worst (Tassi and Muzet 2000).
- Your body that night: HRV and sleeping heart rate against your usual, and skin temperature once the Google Health API supplies it. They are measured during the same night and partly shaped by the sleep itself, and by things the app cannot see, such as alcohol or stress. They mark nights rather than cause them.

# What it cannot do
- It finds patterns, not causes. Something unmeasured that travels with a factor (late nights in stressful weeks, say) is credited to it. More nights shrink the noise but never remove this; only trying a change on purpose, on alternate weeks, can.
- Nights with two or more vitals outside their usual range are left out. They often mean an illness starting, which would otherwise pass for the effect of the training before it.
- Effects are averages over your nights. One bad night after a hard day proves nothing either way.

# How many nights it takes
Estimates start at 30 nights (30 rated mornings for feeling rested) and grow surer with every night. In simulations of this method, with nights about 10 points off what the model expects, a factor became clear four times in five after:
- 8 points per typical change: about 2 months; a yes-or-no factor of that size on a third of your nights, about 6 months.
- 5 points: about 4 months; yes-or-no, about a year.
- 3 points: about a year; yes-or-no, longer.

Most day-to-day influences on sleep are small within a person (Atoui 2021), so expect few clear factors in the first months. On pure noise, fewer than 1 factor in 100 came out clear.

# Model
For each outcome, night $i$ has the outcome $y_i$ and factors $x_{ij}$, each centred on its median and divided by its typical change (its interquartile range; a yes-or-no factor is 0 or 1):

$$y_i = \alpha + \sum_{j} \beta_j x_{ij} + \varepsilon_i$$

$$\varepsilon_i \mid \omega_i \sim N(0,\, \sigma^2/\omega_i)$$

$$\omega_i \sim \mathrm{Gamma}(\nu/2,\, \nu/2), \quad \nu = 4$$

So the errors follow Student's t: a night far off the line gets a small weight $\omega_i$ instead of pulling the estimates (Lange, Little and Taylor 1989).

# Priors
$$p(\alpha) \propto 1, \quad p(\sigma^2) \propto 1/\sigma^2$$

$$\beta_j \mid \sigma^2, \tau \sim N(0,\, \tau^2 \sigma^2)$$

$$p(\tau) \propto \frac{1}{1 + (\tau / 0.5)^2}$$

Every effect starts at zero. The spread $\tau$ is shared by all factors and measured in units of the night-to-night noise; it takes 41 values from 0.02 to 2, evenly spaced in $\ln \tau$, each weighted by its half-Cauchy prior (Gelman 2006). Sharing it lets the factors borrow strength from each other, which is the Bayesian answer to testing many factors at once (Gelman, Hill and Yajima 2012).

# Posterior
With the weights $W = \operatorname{diag}(\omega_i)$ held fixed, $\tilde{X}$ and $\tilde{y}$ centred on their weighted means, $p$ factors and $n$ nights:

$$\Lambda_\tau = \tilde{X}^\top W \tilde{X} + \tau^{-2} I$$

$$m_\tau = \Lambda_\tau^{-1} \tilde{X}^\top W \tilde{y}$$

$$b_\tau = \frac{1}{2}\left(\tilde{y}^\top W \tilde{y} - m_\tau^\top \Lambda_\tau m_\tau\right)$$

Given $\tau$, each effect follows a scaled Student's t with $n - 1$ degrees of freedom:

$$\beta_j \mid \tau, y \sim t_{n-1}\left(m_{\tau j},\, s_{\tau j}^2\right)$$

$$s_{\tau j}^2 = \frac{2 b_\tau}{n - 1} \left[\Lambda_\tau^{-1}\right]_{jj}$$

Each value of $\tau$ is weighted by its prior and its marginal likelihood:

$$w_\tau \propto p(\tau)\, \tau^{1-p} \left|\Lambda_\tau\right|^{-1/2} b_\tau^{-(n-1)/2}$$

(the extra $\tau$ because the grid is even in $\ln \tau$). One eigendecomposition $\tilde{X}^\top W \tilde{X} = Q D Q^\top$ serves every $\tau$:

$$\Lambda_\tau^{-1} = Q \left(D + \tau^{-2} I\right)^{-1} Q^\top$$

# Robust weights
The weights come from expectation-maximisation, repeated until they settle, with $r_i$ night $i$'s residual and $\hat{\sigma}^2$ the posterior estimate of $\sigma^2$:

$$\omega_i = \frac{\nu + 1}{\nu + r_i^2 / \hat{\sigma}^2}$$

# Nights in a row
Nights that follow each other are not independent. With $\rho_e$ the lag-one autocorrelation of the residuals and $\rho_j$ that of factor $j$, the spread of $\beta_j$ is widened when $\rho_e \rho_j > 0$ (Bartlett 1935):

$$\kappa_j = \sqrt{\frac{1 + \rho_e \rho_j}{1 - \rho_e \rho_j}}$$

# Clear or not
This is not a t-test with a p-value. The posterior of each effect is a mixture of Student's t distributions, and from it comes the probability that the effect exceeds the minimum $\delta$ (1 point of score, 0.1 of the rating):

$$P_j^{+} = \sum_\tau w_\tau \left[1 - F_{n-1}\!\left(\frac{\delta - m_{\tau j}}{\kappa_j s_{\tau j}}\right)\right]$$

where $F_{n-1}$ is Student's t distribution function, and $P_j^{-}$ likewise below $-\delta$. A factor is clear when the larger of the two is at least 0.9: a region of practical equivalence decision (Kruschke 2018). The bar spans the 10th to 90th percentile of the mixture, found by bisection.

# Does it predict?
The model must also predict nights it has not seen better than their plain average. Leaving night $i$ out, its prediction error follows from the hat matrix without refitting:

$$e_{(i)} = \frac{y_i - \hat{y}_i}{1 - h_{ii}}$$

$$h_{ii} = \omega_i \left(\frac{1}{\sum_k \omega_k} + \tilde{x}_i^\top \Lambda_\tau^{-1} \tilde{x}_i\right)$$

The weighted mean of $e_{(i)}^2$ must be below that of the average alone; for the night and body factors, also below that of the model of the day before.

# Before and during the night
Factors before the night are fitted alone, which gives their total effects: a late session that shortens sleep shows its whole cost. The night's measures and the body measures are fitted together with them, so they show what goes with a night beyond what the day explains.

# Checked by simulation
On pure noise (6 factors, 30 to 365 nights, 300 runs each), 0.2 to 0.6 % of factors came out clear. A factor planted at 5 points per typical change, with 10 points of noise, came out clear in 45 % of runs at 60 nights, 80 % at 120 and 98 % at 270.
Estimates start once there are enough nights to tell a pattern from chance.

resources.string: Each dot is a night, with the other factors held at their usual values, so that only this factor differs. The line is the estimate.

# Sleep need
Unless set in Settings, the need $N$ is the median time asleep $A$ over the 30 nights up to the night, kept within 7 to 9 hours:

$$N = \min\left(9\,\mathrm{h},\; \max\left(7\,\mathrm{h},\; \operatorname{median} A\right)\right)$$

# Grading
Each measure $v$ has a best value $b$, a threshold $t$ and a worst value $w$, in whichever direction is better:

$$g(v) = \begin{cases} 1 & b \text{ or better} \\ 0.6 + 0.4\,\dfrac{v - t}{b - t} & t \text{ to } b \\ 0.6\,\dfrac{v - w}{t - w} & w \text{ to } t \\ 0 & w \text{ or worse} \end{cases}$$

- Duration $A / N$: $b = 1$, $t = 0.85$, $w = 0.6$.
- Minutes awake after falling asleep: $b = 5$, $t = 20$, $w = 50$ (Ohayon 2017).
- Awakenings of 5 minutes or more: $b = 0$, $t = 1$, $w = 4$.

# Score
$$C = \frac{2\, g_{\mathrm{awake}} + g_{\mathrm{long}}}{3}$$

$$S = 60\, g_{\mathrm{duration}} + 40\, C$$

rounded; a night without stages scores $100\, g_{\mathrm{duration}}$. Good from 80, fair from 65.

Over the 14 days up to the morning (at least 5 nights), each part is graded with $g$ as in the sleep score (threshold 60 %, best 100 %):

# Regularity
For each pair of consecutive nights, the share of the 1,440 minutes from noon on in which the state (asleep or awake) is the same 24 hours later; with at least 4 pairs (Phillips 2017):

$$a_d = \frac{1}{1440} \sum_{m=1}^{1440} \left[s_m = s_{m + 1440}\right]$$

$$\mathrm{SRI} = 200\, \bar{a} - 100$$

graded with $b = 87$, $t = 74$, $w = 50$.

# Duration
The mean of $A / N$: $b = 1$, $t = 0.9$, $w = 0.75$.

# Continuity
The median night's minutes awake after falling asleep: $b = 5$, $t = 20$, $w = 50$.

# Timing
The usual middle of the night is the circular median of the nights' midpoints $m_i$, with $\delta$ the distance round the clock:

$$\tilde{m} = \argmin_{c \in \{m_i\}} \sum_i \delta(m_i, c)$$

graded by its minutes outside 02:00 to 04:00: $b = 0$, $t = 60$, $w = 150$.

# Score
$$H = \frac{100}{K} \sum_{k=1}^{K} g_k$$

over the $K$ parts that could be measured.

Each score and each answer is replaced by its rank, tied values sharing the mean of their ranks. Spearman's $\rho$ is Pearson's correlation of the ranks $R_i$ (scores) and $Q_i$ (answers):

$$\rho = \frac{s_{RQ}}{\sqrt{s_{RR}\, s_{QQ}}}$$

$$s_{RQ} = \sum_i \left(R_i - \bar{R}\right)\left(Q_i - \bar{Q}\right)$$

and $s_{RR}$, $s_{QQ}$ likewise. Without any real association,

$$t = \rho \sqrt{\frac{n - 2}{1 - \rho^2}}$$

roughly follows Student's t with $n - 2$ degrees of freedom; exact tables put the two-sided 5 % limit at $|\rho| = 0.65$ for 10 mornings and 0.36 for 30. The card shows the strength in words and leaves the test out.

The nights of the last 28 days are split into nights before free days ($F$) and before workdays ($W$). For each group, from the mean time of falling asleep $\bar{o}$ and of waking $\bar{w}$:

$$\mathrm{MS} = \frac{\bar{o} + \bar{w}}{2}, \quad \mathrm{SD} = \bar{w} - \bar{o}$$

With $f$ free days a week, the average sleep duration over a week is

$$\overline{\mathrm{SD}} = \frac{(7 - f)\, \mathrm{SD}_W + f\, \mathrm{SD}_F}{7}$$

The chronotype is mid-sleep on free days corrected for catching up (Roenneberg 2004), applied when $\mathrm{SD}_F > \mathrm{SD}_W$:

$$\mathrm{MSF}_{\mathrm{sc}} = \mathrm{MS}_F - \frac{\mathrm{SD}_F - \overline{\mathrm{SD}}}{2}$$

$$\mathrm{SJL} = \left|\mathrm{MS}_F - \mathrm{MS}_W\right|$$

At least 3 workday and 2 free nights are needed.
